summary: Describes a framework for using YANG data models to automate the management of services and networks over their life cycle. Models can produce configuration for components and describe the state to monitor, helping with tasks such as service instantiation and provisioning.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8969 describes how network operators can use YANG data models to connect a customer's service request to network and device configuration. It also explains how operational information can help operators check and adjust a service.

subtitle: How YANG models can connect service requests to network configuration and monitoring.

tldr.problem: Service providers often pass customer requests between separate systems that use different data formats. This can require manual configuration and leave service teams with limited information about network state.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes an operator framework that layers YANG service, network, and device models, then maps and decomposes information between them during service delivery and operation.
tldr.outcome: This Informational document gives an architectural framework and examples. It does not define the communication protocol between a customer and provider or require that every model come from the IETF.

today: RFC 8969 is an Informational framework for service and network management automation. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Management Problem
sections.content:
Service management can involve separate Operations Support System and Business Support System applications, sometimes run by different departments. The RFC says that a lack of standard data inputs and outputs makes integration difficult and can lead to manual configuration. Limited visibility into network state can also slow a response to network changes.

RFC 8969 describes a framework for using YANG models in service and network management. It takes the network operator's perspective and can use models developed by the IETF or other organizations. The framework is architectural guidance, not a definition of the customer-to-provider communication protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate management systems may describe the same service in different ways. The RFC explains how shared data models can help connect those systems and reduce manual steps.

sections.title: Service, Network and Device Models
sections.content:
The framework groups YANG data models into service, network and device levels. A service model describes a service in terms relevant to a customer, such as its communication scope or performance requirements. A network model describes network resources and protocols across devices. A device model describes a device or a function within it, often using technology-specific details.

Models at different levels can be reused and mapped to one another. For example, service requirements can be translated into network parameters and then into configuration for network elements. An orchestrator works with service-level requests, while controllers and devices handle lower-level network and device models. The RFC does not require a particular physical placement for these components.
sections.plainLanguage: A service model records what service is requested. Network and device models describe how the operator can provide it using its infrastructure.

sections.title: Managing a Service Over Time
sections.content:
The service life cycle includes exposing available services, creating or modifying a service, assuring that it meets requirements, optimizing it, diagnosing problems, and decommissioning it. A service request can be checked against available resources and mapped to technology-specific network or device models. When a service ends, its allocated network resources can be released.

Monitoring data can support assurance and optimization. Management systems can compare reported performance with service requirements and update network configuration when conditions or requirements change. At the device level, configuration validation checks whether intended settings took effect; monitoring and diagnostic operations help identify network faults.
sections.plainLanguage: Models can guide setup, changes, monitoring, troubleshooting, and removal of a service. Monitoring data can help an operator decide whether network configuration needs to change.

sections.title: Security Across Model Layers
sections.content:
Network management protocols that access YANG models need secure transport and access control. The RFC identifies SSH as the mandatory secure transport for NETCONF and TLS over HTTPS for RESTCONF. The NETCONF access control model can restrict users to selected protocol operations and data.

When information moves between model layers or is combined from different sources, operators need authentication and authorization checks to prevent inappropriate disclosure. The framework also calls for monitoring the perceived service and comparing it with information from lower layers, so that a mismatch can be investigated.
sections.plainLanguage: Management data needs protection while it moves between systems. Operators also need to control who can see or change that data and check that reported service behavior matches expectations.
